video_title: Simulating Humanity: from Generative Agents to 8 Billion Digital Twins — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI
gist: Joon Sung Park, creator of the 2023 'Generative Agents' (Smallville) paper, discusses building Simile, a startup that creates statistically-validated digital twins of real people (85% behavioral-replication accuracy vs. roughly 20-60% for off-the-shelf frontier LLMs) for enterprise decision simulation, and lays out the company's proprietary data strategy, product model, customer base, and long-term ambition to simulate all 8 billion people on Earth to tackle problems like climate change.

themes.theme: Origins of Generative Agents & Founding Thesis

insights.claim: Simile's founding vision emerged from a 'time machine' thought exercise at Stanford in 2020, where researchers imagined the most impactful application of GPT-3-class models a decade out and concluded that recreating a simulated version of human society was the most ambitious possible use case.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park (guest, CEO Simile)
insights.so_what: Signals the company's founding thesis was chosen for maximal ambition/moonshot potential rather than incremental product-market fit, explaining its hybrid research-lab-plus-company structure.
insights.quote: we played this game that we call the time machine game imagine we were to get on a time machine and fast forward 10 years and look back what would have been the single application that would have mattered

insights.claim: The runner-up idea to full-society simulation at Simile's founding was building fully automated personal-assistant agents, but Park bet that an accurate model of the user must exist before a useful personal-assistant agent can work well.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Implies today's AI personal-assistant products are capped in usefulness until they incorporate deep behavioral models of their users -- an investable gap adjacent to the assistant/agent market.
insights.quote: if you were to create a really amazing personal assistant out of this technology. What you actually need first is an amazing motor of your users.

insights.claim: Park's 2023 Stanford paper 'Generative Agents' (the 'Smallville' paper) is widely cited as one of the best AI papers of that year and has racked up 72,000 reads/citations on Google Scholar as noted in conversation.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Establishes Park's research pedigree as a proof point that Simile's underlying memory-and-agent architecture approach is technically influential and well-regarded academically.
insights.quote: Google Scholar has 72,000.

insights.claim: The Generative Agents memory architecture deliberately avoided knowledge graphs or bespoke trained models in favor of storing everything in markdown/text files, reasoning that LLMs are already strong at parsing and reasoning over text -- the same design pattern later adopted by modern coding-agent products.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Validates markdown-based memory as an emerging industry-standard pattern for agent memory, though Park flags real retrieval-scaling limits once data volume grows large.
insights.quote: just put everything in a markdown file or text file you're done

insights.claim: Park argues current AI assistants (naming ChatGPT/Claude-style products) have not yet delivered a truly useful personal-assistant experience, despite meaningful recent progress, because they still lack a sufficiently deep model of the individual user.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A direct critique from a domain expert of leading consumer AI assistants -- suggests the user-personalization layer remains a wide-open startup opportunity.
insights.quote: I don't think we've actually seen a true personal assistant that's actually useful uh in ways that actually meets the ambition of that particular line of work.

insights.claim: Park's rule of thumb is that fine-tuning/post-training a model's parameters is necessary only when an agent must learn genuinely new 'social physics' it hasn't encountered before; when the model already has the right base statistics, prompting is sufficient to elicit correct behavior.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete decision rule for when to fine-tune vs. prompt-engineer in applied-AI products, directly relevant to the broader post-training-vs-RAG debate in AI infra.
insights.quote: I don't think the model has yet at least the models that are out in the open has yet learned the complete mapping of social physics of humanity.

insights.claim: Simile's core thesis is that frontier LLMs are trained overwhelmingly on self-reported 'attitudinal' web data (social media, Wikipedia) rather than real behavioral data, leaving them missing what Park calls the 'dark knowledge' of how people actually act versus what they say online.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Frames the core product moat: proprietary behavioral data, not more web text, is the scarce resource for accurate human simulation -- a data-moat argument relevant to any 'digital twin' competitor.
insights.quote: they are fundamentally the selfexposed attitudinal data with some behavioral data that sprinkle around here and there. And it has yet to learn really deep behavioral nature of people.

insights.claim: Simile organizes its proprietary training data into three buckets: (1) long-form qualitative life-story interviews, (2) observational behavioral data such as transactions and scraped web activity, and (3) causal/mechanism data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) -- with RCT data considered the rarest and most valuable because it isolates cause and effect in human decisions.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A reusable data taxonomy for evaluating any 'synthetic human' or behavioral-AI startup's data moat and defensibility.

insights.claim: Simile runs its own paid randomized controlled trials in physical and virtual labs (e.g., real e-commerce purchases with real delivered items) specifically to obtain causal behavioral data that can't be scraped from the web, since real-world RCTs are inherently rare -- 'the world is our ground truth, but it happens once.'
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Indicates a genuine data-collection cost/moat (lab plus incentive infrastructure) that is hard for pure-LLM competitors to replicate cheaply.
insights.quote: the world is our ground truth, but it happens once.

insights.claim: Park says customers rarely want pure prediction of an outcome (e.g., 'your sales will drop'); what they actually want from simulation is a step-by-step causal path showing what intervention changes the future outcome, which is why he frames simulation as fundamentally different from forecasting.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Reframes the product category away from prediction-market/forecasting competitors and toward decision-support/intervention-design tools -- relevant when comparing Simile to forecasting startups.
insights.quote: It doesn't really help you to hear that your sales is going to tank in two quarters. They're just going to say, "Wow, that sucks."

insights.claim: Park illustrates the 'path, not outcome' idea with a real EV-marketing example: optimizing narrowly for one metric (EV sales) via simulation can reveal that an intuitive marketing message actually damages perception of the company's gas-powered models and hurts overall sales -- a counterintuitive insight only multi-step simulation surfaces.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A concrete illustrated use case (auto/EV marketing) where naive single-metric optimization backfires -- a caution for companies relying on simple A/B testing instead of systemic simulation.
insights.quote: you can market your EV in XYZ way but that might change people's perception around the cars that's not EV and actually make your overall sales to go down.

insights.claim: The host notes Shopify is building a comparable simulation tool ('Sim Jim,' discussed with Shopify's ML lead in a separate Latent Space episode) aimed at finding non-obvious interventions across a multi-step shopping trajectory, suggesting multiple well-funded companies are independently converging on agent-based behavioral simulation.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Signals a competitive/parallel-innovation landscape around 'simulate the customer journey' tooling -- worth tracking Shopify's internal simulation investment as an adoption bellwether.

themes.theme: Validation, Evals & Accuracy vs. Frontier LLMs

insights.claim: In Simile's benchmark paper 'Generative Simulations of a Thousand People' (published end of 2024), digital twins built from roughly two hours of interview and behavioral data per person replicated those same individuals' behavior on personality tests, economic games, the General Social Survey, and published PNAS randomized controlled trials with 85% accuracy -- matching how consistently people replicate their own past answers.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: This is the core proof point for Simile's product credibility; the 85% figure is the headline metric used to benchmark against alternative synthetic-panel approaches.
insights.quote: we basically could replicate people's behaviors and attitudes 85% as accurately as people would replicate their own

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf frontier LLMs, not fine-tuned on Simile's behavioral data, predict individual human behavior far less accurately than Simile's models -- dropping to roughly 20-30% accuracy on niche/specific populations and only about 50-60% on general-population questions, which Park says is too unreliable for real decisions.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Quantifies the performance gap that justifies Simile's proprietary post-training approach over prompting general-purpose models for synthetic panels -- a moat argument against DIY 'prompt a persona' alternatives.
insights.quote: the model performance of frontier models go all the way down to 20 30%

insights.claim: Frontier chat models are optimized to act as 'super-rational, objective machines' trained partly via professional annotators, whereas modeling authentic human behavior requires the model to reproduce ordinary people's actual irrationality and mistakes -- an explicit inversion of typical LLM alignment objectives.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A structural reason why general-purpose 'smart' LLMs are the wrong base for behavioral simulation -- implies value in specialized post-training that intentionally reduces optimality to match real human decision noise.
insights.quote: the models that we're talking about here what we're trying to create are models that are as dumb as I am right so if I makes those mistakes the motor has to make the same kind of mistake

insights.claim: In a follow-up study, Simile post-trained a model using tens of thousands of pre-registered randomized controlled trials sourced from the Open Science Foundation platform (built partly to combat social science's replication crisis) and found that ingesting this well-designed causal-experiment data significantly improved the model's ability to predict human behavior.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Evidence that curated causal/RCT datasets, not just more generic text scale, are a key lever for improving behavioral-prediction accuracy -- an important input for anyone building synthetic-human or agent-based forecasting tools.

insights.claim: Simile trains two distinct model types for its work -- a population-level model and a harder, more emphasized individual-level model -- both taking a description of a (sub)population or individual plus a stimulus as input.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Clarifies the technical product architecture, useful for benchmarking against competitors that may only build coarse population-level personas rather than individually calibrated digital twins.

insights.claim: Park critiques large-scale 'cross-matrix' synthetic-persona approaches (combining every profession with every demographic background into prompts) as admirable in scale but reliant entirely on statistics already baked into the base LLM's pretraining -- arguing that if this approach truly worked, the simulation problem would already be solved, which it isn't.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A direct competitive critique of cheap persona-prompting approaches to synthetic panels, arguing they can't match Simile's bespoke-data-collection approach on niche/detailed population accuracy -- relevant when evaluating rival synthetic-data vendors.
insights.quote: You're at that point merely retrieving the knowledge that is already embedded in the model in the model parameters.

insights.claim: Simile's core product loop lets customers query synthetic populations by specifying a 'filter' (a description of the target population, e.g. Californians in their 20s-30s) and an 'environment' (a survey, AB test, or behavioral experiment), commonly used for concept testing, virtual focus groups, and simulated public-company earnings calls.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Defines the concrete product surface area investors should evaluate against market-research incumbents; the earnings-call simulation use case is a distinctive, higher-value application worth tracking.

insights.claim: Simile has a strategic partnership with Gallup extending into policy research, but has deliberately not yet built a political-simulation vertical despite clear customer demand, citing concerns about the societal impact and reputational risk of applying synthetic-population modeling to politics.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Signals a large unaddressed demand pocket (political polling/simulation) that Simile is intentionally leaving on the table for governance reasons -- a potential opening for a less risk-averse competitor.
insights.quote: I do see politics as an area where a company has to be particularly thoughtful about the way they operate and make impact.

insights.claim: Wealthfront was one of Simile's first customers to push beyond simple survey-style testing into multimodal product testing, where agents navigate Figma mockups and live websites to simulate real user interaction with a product interface.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Demonstrates an emerging use case -- agentic UI/UX testing with synthetic users -- that could expand Simile's addressable market beyond survey replacement into product design/QA workflows.

insights.claim: Park frames traditional market research (a roughly $100 billion global industry) as an inadequate proxy for Simile's total addressable market, arguing simulation's real category is informing every decision made about and for humans, a much larger and harder-to-size opportunity.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A classic 'reframe the TAM' narrative investors should stress-test against actual revenue and contract sizes rather than taking the expansive framing at face value.
insights.quote: market research is a hundred billion dollar industry.

insights.claim: Simile pitches enterprise buyers on an ROI framing rather than a cost-replacement framing: instead of simply being cheaper than traditional market research, the pitch is that better decisions informed by simulation can save or make companies hundreds of millions to billions of dollars relative to the small cost of running the simulation.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Reveals a value-based pricing/sales narrative tied to decision stakes rather than per-survey cost comparison, implying strong margin potential on large enterprise contracts.

insights.claim: Simile is deployed today at 'some of the largest enterprise companies in the world,' with named customers/partners including CVS, Gallup, Deloitte, and Wealthfront, and Park frames the product as supplementing rather than fully eliminating traditional human survey panels.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete customer roster to watch for expansion signals (contract growth, new logos) as a proxy for enterprise traction.

insights.claim: Simile is observing early signs of a scaling law specific to behavioral simulation: more human behavioral data and more compute produce predictable, continued gains in the model's accuracy at simulating and predicting people, mirroring the scaling laws seen in general LLM pretraining.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: If a genuine behavioral-simulation scaling law exists, the category is compute/data-bound in the same way frontier LLMs are, supporting long-run capital intensity and defensibility for whoever holds the most proprietary behavioral data.
insights.quote: we do post train our own model. The thing that we're actually seeing is the early glimpse of scaling law in simulations.

insights.claim: Simile currently collects fresh behavioral data on tens of thousands of people every week and has panel partnerships reaching tens of millions of people globally, but says most enterprise use cases only require modeling hundreds of thousands of people -- coverage of the right niche subpopulation matters more than raw sample size.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Clarifies current operating scale versus the long-term '8 billion people' vision, useful for sizing near-term compute/data costs against the aspirational narrative.

insights.claim: Once a person is modeled as a digital twin, that agent is reusable indefinitely across unrelated future studies because it is domain-agnostic, since durable individual traits like risk tolerance stay stable over time even though situational behaviors change.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Implies strong operating leverage over time -- the cost of building a digital twin is amortized across many future simulation queries rather than being a one-time-use expense.
insights.quote: your risk tolerance doesn't really change over time it's very consistent

insights.claim: Park predicts that within a few years, running a full-scale societal simulation will cost as much as training a frontier foundation model (tens of millions of dollars), arguing the cost would be justified because the societal value -- e.g., simulating a path to solving climate change -- could vastly exceed it, and says he 'would raise the money right now' to fund such a run.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A capital-intensity signal for the sector's future R&D/compute spend -- foreshadows large future fundraising tied explicitly to compute-heavy 'grand simulation' projects.
insights.quote: I would raise the money right now just to run that.

insights.claim: Park argues running simulations is far cheaper than running equivalent real-world studies, citing a Sam Altman/OpenAI-funded universal basic income study in Africa that cost roughly $14 million over about five years and produced essentially one finding (that UBI did not work as hoped), as the kind of study simulation could replicate cheaper and repeatedly.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A concrete real-world cost benchmark ($14M/5 years for one causal finding) quantifying the potential cost savings simulation offers over traditional philanthropically-funded RCT research.
insights.quote: he spent $14 million quite a bit.

insights.claim: Park's long-term ambition for Simile is to build an agent-based simulation of all 8 billion people on Earth capable of helping answer major unsolved 'wicked' coordination problems such as climate change, early-warning signals for democratic collapse, and the historical origins of monetary systems.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Frames Simile's addressable ambition well beyond commercial market research into public-sector/global-coordination applications -- a long-horizon expansion narrative (and moonshot risk) for the company.
insights.quote: can we create a simulation of 8 billion people living on earth. I think that's quite interesting and that really is the vision

insights.claim: Park draws a direct historical lineage from economist Thomas Schelling's 1970s-80s agent-based segregation model -- where a grid of red/blue dots with even a small same-color neighborhood preference produced full societal segregation over time -- to today's LLM-powered agent-based simulations, noting Schelling's work won a Nobel Prize and directly informed real mixed-income housing policy.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Provides a credible academic precedent for how simulation research can translate into real policy influence and prestige, supporting the plausibility of Park's stated ambition to win a Nobel Prize via this technology.
insights.quote: the very small difference actually causes the society to segregate completely over time. This was very counterintuitive for a lot of people.

insights.claim: Park states explicitly that he believes there is a Nobel Prize in economics to be won in the simulation field and would not be surprised if it happened, positioning generative agent-based simulation as heir to Schelling's Nobel-winning agent-based modeling work, which had largely gone dormant from the 1980s-2000s until generative AI reinvigorated it.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A strong personal conviction statement from the founder about the field's academic legitimacy and long-term prestige potential, relevant to talent recruitment and credibility-building strategy.
insights.quote: I also think yes, I mean, I think there's a Nobel Prize to be won there, which wouldn't be surprising.

insights.claim: Simile was co-founded by four people -- Joon Sung Park, Michael Bernstein (a co-author of the original ImageNet paper that helped launch the deep learning revolution), Percy Liang (who coined the term 'foundation model'), and a business co-founder referred to as Laney (a former VC to some of the fastest-growing AI-native companies) -- giving the company a hybrid research-lab-plus-product-company structure.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Founder pedigree (ImageNet co-author, foundation-model term coiner) is a strong technical-credibility signal relevant to team due diligence.

insights.claim: Simile has grown to roughly 60 employees, of whom 15-20% are former labmates from Park's Stanford research group, several of whom had left for OpenAI and Google Gemini before returning to join Simile.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: A talent-density signal (high concentration of a specific elite research lab's alumni pulled back from OpenAI/Google) that investors often weight heavily when assessing early-stage AI research-lab-style startups.
insights.quote: 15% almost 20% of the company population actually are just my labmates from my person's lab

insights.claim: Simile is headquartered in the Mission Rock neighborhood of San Francisco with a newly opened smaller office in New York, and is actively hiring research talent as well as product/infrastructure engineers, drawing several existing hires from Figma, Notion, and Harvey.
insights.speaker: Joon Sung Park
insights.so_what: Concrete hiring/location signal useful for talent-market tracking and competitive intelligence on where applied-AI startups are drawing engineering talent from.
